<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: The Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) is one of six U.S. territories. Despite its status as a U.S. territory, the CNMI has been historically excluded from certain small business programs. Under my leadership as Chairwoman of the Committee, the House approved H.R. 6021, the Northern Mariana Islands Small Business Act, in the 116th Congress. That bill authorized the establishment of a Small Business Development Center in the CNMI and gave the territory access to the Federal and State Technology (FAST) program. The measure was ultimately included in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) of 2021, which became law. In January 2022, CNMI formally established a SBDC.
However, efforts to include the CNMI in the Microloan program were not as successful. The Microloan program, which provides loans of up to $50,000 through nonprofit intermediaries, is designed to help entrepreneurs and very small businesses access capital--especially when they do not qualify for traditional bank financing. Small businesses in the CNMI, particularly those in the tourism, retail, and service industries, would greatly benefit from access to such small dollar loans. These businesses face unique challenges related to the territory's geographic isolation, high shipping and logistics costs, limited access to credit, and a relatively small local consumer base. As a result, they often struggle to secure affordable financing to start or grow their operations.
One of the rules governing the Microloan program is the 1/ 55 rule, which is a statutory requirement requiring the agency to provide the lesser of $800,000 or 1/55 of the available Microloan funding to any state or territory in the first six months of the fiscal year. Modifying the 1/55 rule to 1/56 to include the CNMI would have no practical effect given the current level of funding. Each state or territory would continue to receive $800,000 for the first six months, and remaining funds would be distributed in the third quarter without regard to the rule.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.
